summary.headline: robots.txt disallows PerplexityBot -- and only PerplexityBot -- from every individual listing and experience page, while Perplexity's own other agent and every other retrieval agent remain permitted — critical severity, Remove the PerplexityBot-specific 'Disallow: /rooms/' and 'Disallow: /experiences/' rules, or confirm they reflect a deliberate decision distinct from every other retrieval agent's treatment.

findings.title: robots.txt disallows PerplexityBot -- and only PerplexityBot -- from every individual listing and experience page, while Perplexity's own other agent and every other retrieval agent remain permitted
findings.evidence: Checked every agent named in this audit's reference list against /rooms/<id>: every retrieval agent except PerplexityBot resolves 'allowed' for individual listing pages -- OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, Perplexity-User, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, Bingbot and Applebot all fall through to the permissive wildcard or an explicit allow. PerplexityBot alone carries an explicit, named robots.txt group that adds 'Disallow: /rooms/' and 'Disallow: /experiences/' on top of the same base rule set every other agent's group shares. Notably, Perplexity's own second agent, Perplexity-User, is not blocked -- an inconsistency within one company's two agents that rules out a coherent 'we don't want Perplexity' policy. Separately, ClaudeBot, anthropic-ai and cohere-ai are also blocked from these paths, but per this audit's own classification those are training-corpus agents, and blocking them is a common, defensible policy decision -- correctly not flagged here. PerplexityBot is the one retrieval agent, used for live answer-building rather than model training, blocked from the site's entire core product (individual property listings).

reproduction.command: curl -s https://www.airbnb.com/robots.txt | grep -A3 'User-agent: PerplexityBot' | tail -3; curl -s https://www.airbnb.com/robots.txt | grep -A3 'User-agent: Perplexity-User'
reproduction.observed: PerplexityBot's group includes 'Disallow: /rooms/' and 'Disallow: /experiences/'; no User-agent: Perplexity-User group exists at all (falls to the permissive wildcard)
reproduction.expected: Both of Perplexity's agents treated consistently -- either both permitted on individual listings, or both restricted, so the policy's intent is legible

suggested_action.summary: Remove the PerplexityBot-specific 'Disallow: /rooms/' and 'Disallow: /experiences/' rules, or confirm they reflect a deliberate decision distinct from every other retrieval agent's treatment.
suggested_action.mechanism: This block removes the brand from Perplexity's live answers for any question about a specific property or experience -- the single most common kind of question a user would ask about an Airbnb listing -- while every other assistant's retrieval agent can still access the same content. The asymmetry with Perplexity's own second agent is the strongest signal this is unintentional rather than policy.
steps: Locate the PerplexityBot-specific robots.txt group and compare it against the Perplexity-User group.
Remove the extra Disallow rules unless there is a specific, documented reason to treat PerplexityBot differently from every other retrieval agent.
suggested_action.verification: curl -s https://www.airbnb.com/robots.txt | grep -A30 'User-agent: PerplexityBot' shows the same rule set as OAI-SearchBot or ChatGPT-User.

findings.title: Every page on the domain -- homepage, individual listings, location pages alike -- delivers only a JavaScript-dependent redirect stub with zero real content to a non-executing fetcher
findings.evidence: Every one of the sampled URLs -- the homepage, an individual listing (/rooms/1341434201707792110), a monthly-stay location page (/snovik-slovenia/stays/monthly), and a partner-program listing (/airbnb-friendly/apartments/atlanta-ga) -- returns an identical-shaped HTTP 200 response of roughly 800-900 bytes: a bare HTML document titled 'Redirecting to www.airbnb.co.in' containing a <form method="POST"> whose only trigger is <body onload="document.forms[0].submit()"> -- i.e. the redirect fires only via JavaScript execution. The <noscript> fallback is a manually-clickable button, not an automatic redirect. Confirmed via a real headless browser (Playwright, executing JavaScript): the form submits successfully and lands on https://www.airbnb.co.in/?locale=en with full, real page content. A non-JS-executing fetcher -- which many AI retrieval agents are -- receives only the ~60-70 characters of visible text in the stub ('Redirecting to www.airbnb.co.in') and never reaches any real content, on any page, anywhere on the domain, from this network origin. This is a domain-level geo/locale redirect mechanism, not a defect specific to any one page.

reproduction.observed: <title>Redirecting to www.airbnb.co.in</title> -- an 800-900 byte stub, no listing content
reproduction.expected: The real page content (or a genuine HTTP 301/302 redirect that a non-executing fetcher follows automatically), not a stub requiring JavaScript to proceed

suggested_action.summary: Replace the JavaScript-triggered form-POST domain-switch with a standard HTTP redirect (301/302/307) to the locale-appropriate domain, or serve the real page content directly with locale detected server-side.
suggested_action.mechanism: A non-executing fetcher follows a genuine HTTP redirect status transparently and reaches the destination content; it cannot submit a form that only fires via a JavaScript onload handler. Since a real browser already completes this exact handoff successfully via a POST carrying cookie and locale payload, the same handoff logic can run server-side (or be expressed as a standard redirect with the equivalent query parameters) instead of depending on client-side JavaScript execution as the only path forward.
steps: Identify what server-side logic already determines the correct destination domain (evidently already computed, since the POST payload contains the resolved host and redirect path).
Issue that decision as a standard HTTP redirect status instead of a client-side form auto-submit.
Verify a plain, non-JS-executing request to any page reaches real content (directly, or via a small number of standard redirect hops).
suggested_action.verification: curl -s -A '<any UA>' https://www.airbnb.com/rooms/<id> returns the real listing content directly, or a Location header pointing to it, rather than a 200 stub requiring JavaScript.

not_assessed.check: Structured data, answerability, freshness, and engagement checks (stages 4-6)
not_assessed.reason: Every sampled page -- across every distinct URL template tried, including the homepage, an individual listing, a location page, and a partner-program page -- returned the identical ~800-900 byte JavaScript-redirect stub described in the delivery finding, with no page-specific content, markup, or text to evaluate. Running these checks against identical stub pages would produce redundant restatements of the same root cause rather than independent observations, so they were not run.
not_assessed.impact: This audit cannot say whether Airbnb's real listing pages (reachable via a JavaScript-executing client) have good structured data, quotable descriptions, current pricing signals, or a good on-site experience -- only that a non-executing fetcher cannot reach that content at all, from this network origin, to check in the first place. Re-running these checks against the JS-rendered destination content (airbnb.co.in, or airbnb.com from a network origin that does not trigger the domain-switch) would be needed for a real read on those stages.

not_assessed.check: Off-site corroboration and entity ambiguity (freshness-corroboration-audit, checks 4-5)
not_assessed.reason: Not performed in this run to stay within the demonstration's time budget.
not_assessed.impact: Not a meaningful concern for an entity as globally well-known as Airbnb, but genuinely not checked.

not_assessed.check: Exact prevalence of the /rooms/ template within the site's full page inventory
not_assessed.reason: The sitemap-derived candidate set (61,680 URLs, capped by this audit's sitemap-fetch budget) was dominated by /stays/monthly location-aggregator pages; individual /rooms/<id> listing pages were present but their exact share of the site's true total page count could not be determined from the capped sample.
not_assessed.impact: The PerplexityBot finding's prevalence is reported as 'widespread' rather than 'site-wide' to reflect this genuine uncertainty, even though individual listings are unambiguously the site's core content regardless of their precise page-count share.
